presentingComplaint: Oozing from venepuncture sites, new petechiae and worsening abdominal distension over 24 hours
history: Known alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, prior ascites, one previous variceal bleed banded 8 months ago) admitted 3 days ago with fever and diffuse abdominal pain. Over the past 24 hours the nursing staff noted persistent bleeding from every cannula and phlebotomy site, spontaneous gum bleeding, and a rapidly spreading petechial and purpuric rash over the trunk and limbs. He has passed a small amount of dark blood per rectum and urine output has fallen to <20 mL/h. He also developed dusky discolouration of two fingertips. The picture has evolved acutely against a background of chronic liver disease, and the family report he was coagulopathic at baseline but never bled spontaneously before. No new drugs other than routine ward medications; not on anticoagulation.
examination: Toxic, drowsy but rousable, deeply jaundiced. Diffuse petechiae and confluent purpura over trunk and extremities with continued oozing from cannula and arterial-line sites. Mucosal (gingival) bleeding. Two acrocyanotic, cool fingertips suggesting microvascular thrombosis. Tense ascites with shifting dullness, mild hepatic flap. No focal peritonism. Cool peripheries with prolonged capillary refill.

labs.factorVIII: 42% (LOW - key discriminator: consumed in DIC, typically normal/high in cirrhotic coagulopathy)
labs.peripheralFilm: schistocytes (fragmented red cells) present, thrombocytopenia confirmed
labs.ISTH_overt_DIC_score: 6 (≥5 = overt DIC): platelets <50 (2), markedly raised D-dimer (3), fibrinogen <1 g/L (1), prolonged PT

imaging: Bedside ultrasound: moderate ascites, coarse nodular cirrhotic liver, patent portal vein, no new focal collection. CXR clear.
microbiology: Blood cultures and diagnostic ascitic tap sent (results pending); ascitic PMN count awaited to exclude a precipitating infective trigger. No organism identified at time of assessment.
differentialDiagnoses: Variceal / GI bleed with dilutional coagulopathy
finalDiagnosis: Overt disseminated intravascular coagulation (consumptive coagulopathy with simultaneous microvascular bleeding and thrombosis) superimposed on chronic liver disease, ISTH score 6
citations: ISTH - Diagnosis and management of overt DIC (scoring system and guidance) - 2013
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation
BSH (British Society for Haematology) - Diagnosis and management of DIC - 2009
stewardship: Not an antimicrobial-stewardship case per se; management is treat-the-trigger plus haemostatic support. Distinguish overt DIC from stable cirrhotic coagulopathy: DIC shows RAPIDLY FALLING platelets and fibrinogen on serial testing, disproportionately high D-dimer, schistocytes, and a LOW factor VIII (factor VIII is endothelially derived and preserved or elevated in pure liver disease). Support only with active bleeding or planned procedure: platelets if <50 ×10³/µL and bleeding, cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen concentrate for fibrinogen <1.0-1.5 g/L, FFP for global factor deficiency; identify and treat the precipitant (search for occult sepsis such as SBP, malignancy). Avoid routine correction of numbers in the absence of bleeding.
contraindications: Do not give tranexamic acid / antifibrinolytics routinely in DIC - risks catastrophic microvascular thrombosis
Avoid prophylactic transfusion purely to normalise INR/platelets when the patient is not bleeding and no procedure is planned
Therapeutic heparin only in DIC where thrombosis dominates and bleeding risk is acceptable - hazardous here given active haemorrhage
edgeCases: Cirrhotic coagulopathy alone can mimic DIC (low platelets, high INR, low fibrinogen) - the discriminators are a normal/high factor VIII, stable (not falling) trends, and modestly raised D-dimer
Concurrent SBP or gram-negative sepsis can be the DIC trigger yet the diagnosis being tested remains DIC, not the infection
Chronic/compensated DIC of malignancy can present with thrombosis rather than bleeding
expectedMaiK: Overt DIC on top of cirrhosis: consumptive coagulopathy (falling platelets and fibrinogen, very high D-dimer, schistocytes, LOW factor VIII) with combined microvascular bleeding and thrombosis - find and treat the trigger, give targeted haemostatic support only for active bleeding, and do NOT give antifibrinolytics.
expectedNextQuestions: Is there an identifiable DIC trigger - occult sepsis (SBP), malignancy, or ischaemic tissue?
Are platelets and fibrinogen falling on serial samples rather than being stably low?
What is the factor VIII level (low favours DIC over pure liver disease)?
Is the patient actively bleeding or does a procedure require haemostatic correction?
